candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the entire encodedJWT string: the header alg value ('none'), all payload claims, and the trailing empty signature segment. Such two-segment tokens are accepted by getParts (line 192, requires the string to end in '.') and can be produced with the library's own public UnsecuredSigner/JWTEncoder or handcrafted. The attacker also chooses whether to include exp/nbf claims.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The early-return at lines 70-76 (and 125-131) is intended unsecured-JWT support and only triggers when zero verifiers are given; it is not the flaw. Three-part alg=none tokens are correctly rejected via the parts.length == 3 && verifier == null guard (MissingVerifierException, line 160), so the bypass requires the two-part trailing-dot form. Built-in verifiers cannot match Algorithm.none (HMACVerifier 56-65, RSAVerifier 60-70), so verifier is null; a custom Verifier that returned true for none would instead hit the invalid-signature guard at line 164. Jackson maps 'alg':'none' to Algorithm.none (proven by the encoder vector asserted in JWTTest.test_none line 341), and UnsecuredSigner/JWTEncoder (76-82) emit exactly the trailing-dot form. No existing test passes a none token together with a verifier, so no test expectation contradicts the analysis. The private decode does validate exp/nbf (176-184), but these are attacker-supplied claims.
candidates.impact: Authentication/authorization bypass: a forged JWT is returned as a successfully decoded JWT and no Verifier.verify() is ever called, so an application that trusts a decoded token's subject/issuer/role claims can be impersonated without any secret or private key. Because the attacker controls the claims, exp/nbf checks can be omitted, and no cryptographic material is needed.
candidates.prerequisites: The application calls JWTDecoder.decode with at least one Verifier (varargs or Map overload, as in the README usage examples) and passes it attacker-influenced token material. The token must use the two-segment unsecured form ending in '.'. Built-in verifiers do not claim Algorithm.none, so verifier resolves to null.
candidates.root_cause: JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...) rejects two-part unsecured JWTs only inside the branch guarded by verifiers.length == 0 (line 70), and the private decode() rejects a missing signature only when a verifier was resolved (line 164: parts.length == 2 && verifier != null). When verifiers are supplied but none supports Algorithm.none (the built-in HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier.canVerify return false for none), verifier stays null; the parts.length == 3 && verifier == null guard (line 159) does not match a two-part token; the verification block (line 168) is skipped; and the payload is deserialized and returned at line 174 without any Verifier.verify invocation. The Map-based overloads (lines 117-142) have the same fall-through because an absent/unknown kid yields a null verifier.
candidates.title: Unsecured JWT (alg=none) accepted without signature verification when verifiers are supplied
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker submits a token of the form base64url({'alg':'none',...}) + '.' + base64url(claims) + '.'. 2) getParts (189-197) returns 2 parts and accepts it because the string ends with '.'. 3) In decode(String, Verifier...) the guard at line 70 is skipped because verifiers.length != 0. 4) The selection loop (80-84) calls canVerify(Algorithm.none); HMACVerifier (56-65) and RSAVerifier (60-70) return false, so verifier remains null. 5) The private decode() is entered with verifier == null and parts.length == 2: line 159 requires parts.length == 3, line 164 requires verifier != null, and line 168 requires parts.length == 3, so all three guards are bypassed; line 174 deserializes the payload and returns it. 6) Lines 176-184 only reject the token if the attacker supplied exp/nbf, which the attacker simply omits. The same sequence applies to decode(String, Map) (125-142) when the header's kid is absent/unknown and Map.get returns null (HashMap). Result: decode returns attacker-chosen claims with no signature verification.
candidates.unverified: Static reading only; no code, tests, or scanners were executed, so runtime reachability and exploitability were not confirmed. The Map-overload behavior assumes HashMap semantics for a null key (an implementation that rejects null keys, e.g. TreeMap, would throw instead). Applications that pass no verifiers, or that reject alg=none tokens before calling the library, are unaffected. The single file excluded by the sensitive-name filter (likely a test key PEM) and the src/test/resources key files referenced by tests were not available for inspection.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347); acceptance of the JWT 'none' algorithm

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reports 43 root files, 42 model-visible, 1 excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter (not enumerable), no symlinks, no binaries, no >5 MiB files. get_relation_scope reports 40 parsed Java files, 237 symbols, 458 edges, 955 calls, 725 unresolved calls, 19 omitted files, partial index status, and explicitly no control-flow, data-flow, or semantic resolution; index labels were used only for navigation and every cited relation was re-verified in source text. I line-read all 32 main Java files, all 8 test Java files, pom.xml, and README.md, tracing the primary path JWTDecoder -> HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier and JWTEncoder/UnsecuredSigner -> Algorithm/Header/JWT -> Mapper.
limitations: Static review only: no code, tests, or scanners were executed; the candidate is a source-evidenced lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

One of 43 root files is withheld by the sensitive-name/path filter and the src/test/resources rsa_*.pem keys referenced by tests are not present in the visible snapshot, so those files could not be inspected.

The relation index omits 19 files, implements no control/data-flow or semantic resolution, and leaves 725 calls unresolved; behavior of downstream callers outside this repository could not be assessed.
Only the built-in HMAC/RSA verifiers and HashMap-style verifier maps were analyzed; custom Verifier or Map implementations could alter the outcome for the map overload.
README.md and pom.xml are untrusted repository data and were used only as context about intended usage/version, not as proof of behavior.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsecured early-return path skips exp/nbf validation (JWTDecoder.java 70-76 and 125-131) despite the javadoc promising expiry checks
rejected_leads.reason: Real inconsistency, but only reachable when the caller supplies zero verifiers, i.e. has explicitly opted out of signature verification; lower impact and same call path, so not split out as a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HMACVerifier.verify uses Arrays.equals for MAC comparison (HMACVerifier.java 78)
rejected_leads.reason: Potentially non-constant-time comparison, but a practical timing side channel was not demonstrated and the same secret material is required; weaker than the signature bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: Verifier selection loop lacks a break, so the last matching verifier wins, contradicting the javadoc 'first verifier found' (JWTDecoder.java 80-84)
rejected_leads.reason: Behavioral/API inconsistency; no concrete attacker advantage without a specific multi-verifier configuration, and the library still verifies with one of the supplied verifiers.
Test-quality defect that can accept an unexpected supertype exception and mask regressions; test-only, no direct runtime security impact.
Outdated dependency, but Mapper enables no default typing and deserializes into fixed target types, so no polymorphic-deserialization gadget is demonstrated in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: RSAUtils uses sun.security internal classes for PEM parsing (RSAUtils.java 19-21)
rejected_leads.reason: Portability/maintenance concern on a configuration-supplied key path, not a remotely attacker-controlled input.

rejected_leads.lead: JWT claim getters cast/parse values without type checks (JWT.java 181-216)
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker-shaped claims can trigger ClassCastException/NumberFormatException (minor exception-type/DoS concern) but only after decoding, and it is subsumed by the main bypass or by callers that intentionally decode unverified tokens.

summary: Reviewed the prime-jwt 1.3.0 snapshot (42 model-visible files: 32 main Java, 8 test Java, pom.xml, README.md), tracing the JWT decode path end-to-end. The strongest distinct issue is in JWTDecoder.decode: when the caller supplies at least one Verifier, a two-segment unsecured JWT whose header declares alg=none is resolved to verifier==null and then falls through every guard in the private decode(), so the attacker-controlled payload is deserialized and returned with no Verifier.verify() call. The guard that rejects unsecured tokens only applies when verifiers.length==0 (line 70), and the no-signature guard only applies when a verifier was resolved (line 164). This is a signature-verification bypass reachable from all three public decode overloads. No code was executed; the finding is static, source-evidenced, and not runtime-confirmed. Other leads (expiry/nbf skipped on the no-verifier unsecured path, non-constant-time MAC compare, last-matching-verifier selection, reversed isAssignableFrom in the test helper, stale Jackson 2.8.1) were considered and rejected as weaker or non-exploitable on available evidence.
